title: FetchError conflates a TLS validation failure with a network failure
description:
## What

pkix_mta_sts_http::FetchError::Transport(String) carries both:

  - the policy host's certificate did not validate
  - the connection was refused, reset, or never established

as one opaque string, because ureq and reqwest report them as incompatible types and the variant was written to erase that difference.

## Why it matters

The HTTPS certificate is an MTA-STS policy's ONLY authentication. The _mta-sts TXT record is unsigned; the policy body carries no signature. So "the certificate did not validate" means "this policy may have been written by an attacker", and "the connection was refused" means "the domain's web server is down". Those are not the same event and a sender should not treat them alike.

Two concrete consequences:

TLSRPT CANNOT REPORT IT. RFC 8460 §4.3.2.2 defines sts-webpki-invalid as "the MTA-STS Policy could not be authenticated using PKIX validation" -- the most security-relevant thing a report can say about MTA-STS. pkix-tlsrpt cannot produce it, because classifying Transport that way would tell a domain its certificate is broken whenever its policy host is merely down, sending an operator after a certificate that is fine. There is a test in pkix-tlsrpt asserting no FetchError maps to sts-webpki-invalid, so this gap is pinned rather than forgotten.

AN OPERATOR CANNOT ALERT ON IT. §3.3 asks senders to "alert administrators (through the use of logs or similar) when such attempts fail". A deployment that wants to page on "someone may be MITM-ing our policy fetches" but not on "example.com's web server is down" cannot write that rule today.

## What to do

Add a variant -- TlsValidation(String), or similar -- and populate it from each backend:

  ureq     ureq::Error::Io wrapping a rustls error. Needs checking what
           ureq 3 actually surfaces; it may require inspecting the io error's
           source chain for a rustls::Error, which is fragile but at least
           localised to one place.
  reqwest  reqwest::Error has no is_tls(), but the error source chain
           reaches rustls::Error. Same approach.

Both are string- or downcast-matching on a dependency's internals, which is why this was not done inline: it wants a deliberate decision about how fragile a classification is acceptable, and a test per backend that a bad certificate produces the new variant.

If neither backend can distinguish it reliably, that is also an answer -- but then the Transport documentation should say so explicitly, rather than leaving a reader to assume the distinction is available.

## Testing it needs a bad certificate

Which is why this is not trivial: the existing destination-policy tests work because mta-sts.localhost resolves to loopback and is refused before any TLS. Testing a certificate failure needs a TLS listener presenting a certificate that does not validate -- a self-signed cert on a local port, or a known-bad public endpoint such as expired.badssl.com (network-dependent, so #[ignore]d like the resolver's live tests).

## Acceptance

[ ] Decide whether each backend can distinguish a TLS failure reliably, and record the finding
[ ] If yes: a FetchError variant for it, populated from both backends
[ ] A test per backend that a certificate that does not validate yields it, not Transport
[ ] pkix-tlsrpt's classify_fetch_error maps it to sts-webpki-invalid, and the test asserting the gap is updated to assert the mapping instead
[ ] If no: FetchError::Transport's documentation states that the distinction is unavailable and why
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-11-25. FetchError::TlsValidation added; pkix-tlsrpt now produces sts-webpki-invalid. 2265 workspace tests, no failures.

## The finding, which contradicted my own filing

The bead guessed ureq would surface rustls via Error::Rustls and that both backends would need source-chain matching. Probing against expired.badssl.com, self-signed.badssl.com and untrusted-root.badssl.com showed otherwise:

  ureq     Error::Io(io) -> io.get_ref() downcasts to the concrete
           rustls::Error. EXACT, no string matching. It does NOT use its own
           Error::Rustls variant for a peer-certificate failure, which is
           what the filing assumed.
  reqwest  Chain reaches an io::Error whose get_ref() is Some but is an
           OPAQUE wrapper -- not downcastable to rustls::Error, and with no
           further source. Only the rendered string survives.

My first probe reported "downcast=None" for ureq too, which was my bug: I tried downcasting the top-level ureq::Error to io::Error, when Error::Io is a variant rather than an io::Error itself. Worth noting because it nearly led to concluding neither backend could do it exactly.

## What shipped

certificate_failure makes two passes, in order of trustworthiness:

  1. downcast to rustls::Error -- exact; covers every ureq case
  2. rustls's own "invalid peer certificate" Display prefix -- fallback for
     reqwest

The prefix comes from rustls::Error::InvalidCertificate, whose Display is
"invalid peer certificate: {e}". It is specific to CERTIFICATE validation, which is exactly the scope of sts-webpki-invalid ("could not be authenticated using PKIX validation") rather than TLS failures generally -- so the fallback is narrower than it first looks.

Public, for the same reason as check_status: a sender with its own HTTP client must make the same determination, and restating this walk is the duplication that ends with one caller unable to report a man-in-the-middle. Gated on a backend feature since rustls arrives with the client; the VARIANT is unconditional so pkix-tlsrpt classifies it without either backend.

## The negative direction was the point

A false positive would tell a domain its certificate is broken whenever its policy host is unreachable -- which is the specific harm that kept this unimplemented. So the tests assert both ways:

  recognised     expired, self-signed, untrusted-root -- on BOTH backends,
                 asserted separately because reqwest uses the fallback path
                 and a change that worked for ureq could silently leave the
                 async path unable to report sts-webpki-invalid
  NOT recognised refused connection, DNS failure, valid certificate, and a
                 set of near-miss strings ("certificate", "peer certificate",
                 "invalid peer", "tls handshake eof")

The live ones are #[ignore]d so the suite stays offline; they pass with --ignored.

## The pinned gap, inverted rather than deleted

pkix-tlsrpt's test asserting NOTHING maps to sts-webpki-invalid is kept and inverted: only FetchError::TlsValidation maps to it, and Transport explicitly does not. The harm it guards against has not changed -- only the ability to distinguish the cases -- so a future change folding TlsValidation back into Transport, or classifying a network error as a certificate one, still fails there.

That is the pattern worth keeping: when a documented gap gets closed, the test that pinned it becomes the test that holds the fix, rather than being removed with the gap.

## If reqwest ever improves

The exact pass starts catching it and the fallback becomes dead weight rather than a behaviour change. No action needed; nothing to remember.

## Acceptance

[x] Decide whether each backend can distinguish a TLS failure reliably, and record the finding -- ureq exactly, reqwest only by message
[x] A FetchError variant for it, populated from both backends
[x] A test per backend that a certificate that does not validate yields it, not Transport
[x] pkix-tlsrpt's classify_fetch_error maps it to sts-webpki-invalid, and the test asserting the gap is updated to assert the mapping instead
[x] FetchError::Transport's documentation states what it does and does not include
